introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination / Technical and Vocational Education Examination. Citizenship Education 2 (0562), Paper 2, ORDINARY INTERMEDIATE LEVELS, JUNE 2020. Duration: Two and a half (2 1/2) hours.**

Instructions to candidates:

- You are required to answer FOUR questions choosing QUESTION 1 and THREE others from Sections A, B, and C.
- All the questions carry equal marks and marks allocated to different parts of questions are indicated.
- Extra question(s) answered from each section shall NOT be marked.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**Question 1 (compulsory)**

Study this extract on a speech by the Head of State and an article on corruption in Cameroon and then answer questions (a) to (d) that follow. (The maximum marks for each sub-question is indicated in brackets)

> "I am fully determined to eliminate this scourge and to step up the fight against corruption, without complacency, discrimination and irrespective of the political status or political leaning of those found guilty. Nobody will consider himself or herself to be above the law..."

Article 66 of the Cameroon Constitution stipulates thus: "The President of the Republic, the Prime Minister, Members of Government and ... shall declare their assets and property at the beginning and at the end of their tenure of office".

Corruption is a canker worm that has invaded the Cameroonian society. It cuts across all sectors in Cameroon, be it public or private: including the judiciary, police, customs, public service, education and health. Cameroon has twice been classified as the most corrupt nation in the world in 1998 and 1999 by a renowned international N.G.O. Corruption is manifested in several forms including bribery, extortion and tax evasion. It has a serious negative impact on the country's economy and image.

*Source: Cameroon Corruption Report: May 2017*

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) (i) Identify the Head of State mentioned in the extract.

(ii) Which arm of government does the personality mentioned in a(i) above represent?

(iii) State two functions performed by the Head of State.

(v) What relationship exists between the arm of government identified in a(i) above and the judiciary?

[1 + 1 + 2 + 1 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The Head of State [1 mark].** The extract is a speech by the **President of the Republic of Cameroon**, who is the Head of State (at the time of this examination, H.E. Paul Biya, President since 1982).

**(ii) The arm of government [1 mark].** The President represents the **Executive** arm of government (the arm that carries out the laws and runs the country, together with the Prime Minister and the Government).

**(iii) Two functions of the Head of State [2 marks]** (any two):

- He **represents the State** and the nation, at home and abroad (for example he signs and ratifies treaties and accredits ambassadors).
- He is the **guarantor of the Constitution** and ensures the proper functioning of the public institutions.
- He **appoints the Prime Minister, the members of Government** and senior civil and military officials.
- He is the **Head of the armed forces** and ensures national defence and security.
- He **promulgates laws** passed by Parliament and **signs decrees** to apply them.
- He **presides over the Council of Ministers** and defines the policy of the nation.
- He has the **right of pardon** (he may reduce or cancel a sentence).

**(v) Relationship between the Executive and the Judiciary [1 mark]** (the fourth part, printed (v) in the paper). The two arms are **separate and the judiciary is independent**: the courts judge cases according to the law and not according to the wishes of the Executive. However, the two **cooperate**: the President of the Republic is the guarantor of the independence of the judiciary and appoints magistrates with the help of the Higher Judicial Council, and the Executive enforces court decisions (through the police, gendarmerie and prisons). The judiciary also checks that the Executive acts within the law, which is why "nobody is above the law".
themes: separation of powers and arms of government

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) (i) What is the meaning of the phrase "corruption is a canker worm..." as mentioned in the extract?

(ii) Identify any two important institutions created by the Cameroon Government to fight against corruption in the country.

(iii) From which Constitution is Article 66 mentioned in the extract above taken?

[1 + 2 + 1 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Meaning of the phrase [1 mark].** A canker worm is an insect pest that secretly eats and destroys plants from inside. By calling corruption a "canker worm", the writer means that corruption is a **harmful, hidden and destructive evil that slowly eats away and spreads through the whole of society** (all sectors, public and private) and damages the economy and the country's image.

**(ii) Two anti-corruption institutions [2 marks]** (any two):

- The **National Anti-Corruption Commission (CONAC)**, which receives complaints, investigates and prevents corruption.
- The **National Agency for Financial Investigation (ANIF)**, which tracks suspicious financial transactions such as money laundering.
- The **Special Criminal Court**, which tries cases of large-scale embezzlement of public funds.
- The **Supreme State Audit (CONSUPE)** and the **Audit Bench of the Supreme Court**, which control the use of public money.
- Anti-corruption units in ministries and public bodies.

**(iii) The Constitution [1 mark].** Article 66 is taken from the **Constitution of Cameroon of 18 January 1996** (the Constitution now in force, which amended the 1972 Constitution).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) (i) Suggest two reasons for rampant corruption in Cameroon.

(ii) Write down in full the initials 'N.G.O' as mentioned in the extract.

(iii) Apart from the Government, which other bodies are involved in the fight against corruption in Cameroon?

[2 + 1 + 2 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Two reasons for rampant corruption [2 marks]** (any two):

- **Low salaries and poverty**: some workers ask for "extra" payments to make ends meet.
- **Greed and love of money**: the wish to become rich quickly.
- **Weak punishment and impunity**: people who are caught are not always sanctioned, so others are encouraged.
- **Lack of transparency** in the management of public funds and public contracts.
- **Poor moral and civic education**, and the bad example of some leaders.
- **Social pressure** from family and friends who expect gifts or favours.

**(ii) N.G.O. [1 mark].** **Non-Governmental Organisation.**

**(iii) Other bodies fighting corruption [2 marks]** (any two):

- **Non-governmental organisations and civil society associations**, which sensitise the public, denounce corrupt practices and monitor public spending.
- **The media** (press, radio, television), which investigate and expose corruption.
- **Religious bodies** (churches, mosques), which teach honesty and moral values.
- **Trade unions, schools and youth groups**, which educate their members.
- **International organisations and partners**, which support anti-corruption programmes and audits.
- **Ordinary citizens**, who refuse to give bribes and report corrupt acts.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) (i) Identify other forms of corruption in Cameroon not mentioned in the extract.

(ii) Briefly describe other social ills other than corruption which continue to plague Cameroon today?

[2 + 4 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Other forms of corruption [2 marks].** The extract mentions bribery, extortion and tax evasion. Others are (any two):

- **Embezzlement** (misappropriation) of public funds.
- **Nepotism, favouritism and tribalism** in recruitment and promotion.
- **Examination malpractice** and "sexually transmitted marks" in schools.
- **Fraud and forgery** (false documents, ghost workers, overpricing of contracts).
- **Abuse of office** and illegal commissions ("kickbacks") on public contracts.
- **Electoral fraud** (buying votes).

**(ii) Other social ills [4 marks]** (any four, each briefly described):

- **Unemployment**: many young graduates and school leavers cannot find work, which leads to frustration and crime.
- **Poverty**: many families cannot afford food, health care or school fees.
- **Crime and insecurity**: theft, armed robbery and kidnapping threaten people and property.
- **Drug and alcohol abuse**: harms the health and future of young people.
- **HIV/AIDS and other diseases**: weaken families and the workforce.
- **Child abuse, child labour and child trafficking**: deprive children of their rights and education.
- **Road accidents**: cause many deaths and injuries every year.
- **Illiteracy and school dropout**, especially among girls in some areas.
- **Prostitution and moral decay**, linked to poverty and weak family control.
